paragraphs: The paper connects two accounts of animal behavior: learning to obtain rewards from the outside world and regulating the body's internal condition. Reinforcement learning describes behavior through reward maximization, while homeostatic regulation describes it through reducing departures from physiological setpoints. The authors ask how these objectives can fit into one analytical framework.

Their approach builds on drive-reduction theory, linking reward to the reduction of physiological need. Within the proposed framework, maximizing reward and maintaining physiological stability become equivalent objectives. This provides a way to describe behavioral adaptation using both the animal's internal state and the external circumstances in which it acts.

The authors also show how this framework can jointly explain several behavioral phenomena: changes in associative learning with motivation, anticipatory responses, competition between motivational systems, and risk aversion. The contribution is a theoretical connection that gives these phenomena a shared explanation. The equivalence belongs to the proposed model, rather than establishing that every form of animal reward necessarily serves physiological regulation.
neurips-2011-a-reinforcement-learning-th.tldr: A drive-reduction framework makes reward maximization and physiological stability equivalent within one theory of learning and regulation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose the settings that determine how a learning algorithm is trained. Its motivation is that better configurations of existing methods can produce substantial improvements without changing the underlying feature-learning approach. As computing resources permit more trials, automated search becomes an increasingly useful alternative to manual tuning.

The authors evaluate random search and introduce two greedy sequential methods based on expected improvement. These methods select further configurations using a model of how settings relate to performance. A central contribution is handling conditional relevance: some settings matter only when other settings take particular values, so the search model must represent that structure.

The experiments concern neural networks and deep belief networks. Although random search had proved sufficiently efficient for neural networks on several datasets, the authors find it unreliable for deep belief networks. Their sequential methods obtain significantly better results on difficult deep-belief-network problems than those previously reported. These findings show why a search strategy that works in one training setting may need a more structured replacement in another.
neurips-2011-algorithms-for-hyper-parame.tldr: Two sequential hyper-parameter search methods handle conditional settings and improve difficult deep-belief-network results where random search is unreliable.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods learn how to act by estimating which changes to a policy would increase reward. They can operate without a model of the environment, but their gradient estimates can vary substantially. This paper investigates that variability and develops an improvement intended to make the estimates more stable.

The analysis focuses on policy gradients with parameter-based exploration, or PGPE, and compares it with the classical REINFORCE method. Under a mild assumption, the authors prove that PGPE has lower gradient-estimation variance. They then derive an optimal baseline for PGPE, a reference used in the estimator to reduce its variability further.

The comparison also covers versions of both methods equipped with their optimal baselines. The authors theoretically favor PGPE on the variance criterion and report experiments demonstrating the usefulness of the improved method. The result concerns the stability of the learning signal: less variable estimates provide a clearer indication of how to adjust the policy. The abstract's theoretical advantage is specifically about variance, with the initial comparison subject to its stated assumption.
neurips-2011-analysis-and-improvement-of.tldr: The paper establishes variance advantages for PGPE and derives an optimal baseline that further stabilizes its policy-gradient estimates.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weak learners into a strong classifier, but training can become expensive when there are very many examples and features. Sampling either examples or features can reduce computation. The paper asks a more specific question: given a fixed time budget, how should that computation be allocated to reduce training loss most effectively?

The authors analyze the trade-off between inspecting more examples and considering more features. They use that analysis to design algorithms that estimate a suitable allocation during every boosting iteration. The target is the greatest expected reduction in loss, so the sampling decision responds to the current learning problem rather than following one fixed allocation throughout training.

Experiments on object recognition using two standard computer-vision datasets show the proposed adaptive methods outperforming basic sampling approaches and state-of-the-art bandit methods. The contribution connects computational savings to learning progress: a faster iteration is useful insofar as it helps improve the classifier within the available time. The algorithms estimate the best trade-off as training proceeds; the reported empirical comparisons support their effectiveness on the evaluated problems.
neurips-2011-boosting-with-maximum-adapt.tldr: Adaptive boosting algorithms choose how many examples and features to inspect at each iteration to maximize expected loss reduction within a time budget.

paragraphs: A model trained in one domain may struggle in another because the data distributions differ. Some features that matter in the target domain may even be absent from the source domain. This paper introduces CODA, a co-training approach that gradually incorporates target information to bridge that gap.

CODA progressively adds target features and target instances about which the current algorithm is most confident. It does not require a predetermined division of features into separate views. Instead, each iteration solves one optimization problem that jointly learns the target predictor, the division into views, and a shared subset of source and target features for the predictor.

On a benchmark containing twelve domains, CODA significantly outperforms the state of the art reported in the abstract. It achieves the best performance in 65 of 84 comparisons spanning no labeled target examples through relatively substantial target supervision. The findings support learning the feature views and the predictor together while gradually expanding the target information used. The results cover varied supervision levels without claiming that CODA wins every comparison.
neurips-2011-co-training-for-domain-adap.tldr: CODA gradually incorporates confident target information while jointly learning feature views and a predictor, improving domain adaptation across varied supervision levels.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization objectives made by adding a smooth convex function to a nonsmooth convex function. Proximal-gradient methods handle these two parts through different computations. In practice, either the gradient calculation for the smooth part or the proximity operation for the nonsmooth part may be approximate, raising the question of how those errors affect convergence.

The authors analyze three settings: the basic method, the basic method under strong convexity, and an accelerated method. They show that each can retain its corresponding error-free convergence rate when the computational errors decrease at a suitable rate. The guarantee therefore links the accuracy required of individual operations to the progress of the overall optimization.

Experiments on a structured sparsity problem indicate that error sequences satisfying these theoretical requirements can also improve practical performance. This makes controlled approximation a useful algorithmic choice rather than merely an unavoidable defect. The key condition is that errors must shrink appropriately; the result does not say that arbitrary inaccuracies preserve convergence speed.
neurips-2011-convergence-rates-of-inexac.tldr: Proximal-gradient methods retain their error-free convergence rates when approximation errors decrease appropriately, with experiments indicating practical benefits.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to place the nodes of a directed graph in Euclidean space while preserving information about edge direction. Its modeling starting point is that the observed graph comes from samples on a manifold equipped with a vector field. This describes both an underlying geometric space and directional structure associated with that space.

The proposed algorithm separates three components of this model: the manifold's geometry, the density with which data are sampled, and the vector field. Treating these as distinct quantities matters because an embedding is intended to represent more than where observations are concentrated. It must also account for the directional information present in the graph.

The method is motivated by analyzing Laplacian-type operators and their continuous limits, which become generators of diffusion processes on the manifold. This supplies a mathematical connection between graph computations and the underlying geometric model. The authors illustrate recovery on artificial and real data. Their contribution is thus a model-based recovery algorithm with a continuous-limit rationale, demonstrated on both kinds of data.
neurips-2011-directed-graph-embedding-an.tldr: A directed-graph embedding method uses a manifold model to separate underlying geometry, sampling density, and directional structure.

paragraphs: The paper approaches anomaly detection by learning minimum-volume sets for the distribution of nominal, or normal, data. Such sets provide a compact description of normal observations. An existing nearest-neighbor graph method offers desirable theoretical properties, but its computational demands motivate simpler ways to estimate these sets.

The authors propose a bipartite nearest-neighbor graph estimator called BP-kNNG. They state that it preserves the desirable theoretical properties of the earlier K-kNNG method while requiring less computation than both that method and its leave-one-out heuristic approximation. The contribution therefore aims to retain the original statistical foundation while making the graph-based calculation more efficient.

A specific theoretical result establishes asymptotic consistency for recovering each test point's p-value. This is a statement about behavior as the available data grow, rather than exact recovery from every finite dataset. Experiments also illustrate superior performance relative to the leave-one-out approximation and other leading anomaly detectors. Together, these findings connect a simpler graph construction with both statistical justification and favorable empirical detection results.
neurips-2011-efficient-anomaly-detection.tldr: A bipartite nearest-neighbor anomaly detector reduces computation while preserving theoretical properties and consistently recovering test-point p-values asymptotically.

paragraphs: The paper asks how the number of units in a restricted Boltzmann machine determines the probability distributions it can represent. The authors identify explicit distribution classes available to models of different sizes. These classes make the model's expressive power concrete by connecting its architecture to the kinds of distributions it can accommodate.

Using that characterization, the authors derive an upper bound on the worst-case Kullback-Leibler divergence to an RBM with n visible units and m hidden units. The stated bound is (n−1)−log(m+1). This expresses an approximation guarantee in terms of architecture size, relating the number of hidden units to a measure of distributional mismatch.

The result allows the authors to specify hidden-unit counts sufficient for a model to contain particular distribution classes while meeting a chosen error tolerance. Its significance is a principled link between model capacity and approximation requirements. A sufficient size guarantee establishes that the architecture is rich enough for the stated purpose; it does not establish that every smaller architecture must fail.
neurips-2011-expressive-power-and-approx.tldr: Explicit representable distribution classes and a worst-case KL bound connect RBM hidden-unit counts to sufficient approximation capacity.

paragraphs: Stratified Monte Carlo integration divides an estimation problem into parts and combines estimates from those parts using weights. The paper studies how to allocate samples when the variability within each part is initially unknown. It casts the strata as arms in a multi-armed bandit problem, with the goal of estimating a weighted average of their means.

The proposed strategy allocates samples according to upper bounds on the arms' standard deviations. It is compared with an ideal allocation that already knows those standard deviations. This comparison isolates the estimation cost of learning how sampling effort should be distributed, rather than assuming the required variability information is available in advance.

The authors provide two finite-time regret bounds. A distribution-dependent bound has order n^(−3/2) and depends on a measure of disparity between arms. A distribution-free bound has order n^(−4/3) and avoids that dependence. These give two complementary guarantees on the gap relative to the informed allocation: one reflects properties of the particular problem, while the other applies without using that disparity measure.
neurips-2011-finite-time-analysis-of-str.tldr: A bandit-based stratified sampling strategy receives finite-time regret bounds against an ideal allocation that knows each stratum's variability.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchical topic model for choices people make over time. A branch of the model's tree corresponds to a type of person, while each node contains probabilities over selectable items. This gives the model a way to describe both broad patterns of choice and more detailed patterns along a branch.

The construction extends the nested Chinese restaurant process and assumes that observations include the times at which choices were made. It deliberately makes deeper topics more likely to be used as time increases. A new change-point stick-breaking model, coupled with Poisson and product-of-gammas components, imposes that temporal structure. A Dirichlet process allows topic distributions to be shared across nodes.

The authors demonstrate the approach using undergraduate course selections at Duke University. Their aim is to reveal and compactly describe structure in both the curriculum and the student population. The temporal progression toward deeper topics is an explicit modeling preference: it shapes how changing choices are represented, rather than being presented as a universal law of personal behavior.
neurips-2011-hierarchical-topic-modeling.tldr: A nonparametric topic tree models personal choices over time by making deeper topics increasingly likely and sharing topics across nodes.

paragraphs: The paper studies image segmentation through correlation clustering, a method for partitioning a graph into groups. It begins with a graph whose nodes are superpixels and whose pairwise relationships inform which regions belong together. The motivation includes the computational burden and manual parameter tuning associated with existing segmentation approaches.

The authors extend this pairwise formulation to a hypergraph that can express relationships involving groups of superpixels. These higher-order relationships improve clustering when local boundaries are ambiguous. The approach allows a segmentation decision to account for a larger grouping, instead of relying exclusively on separate relationships between pairs of regions.

The formulation supports fast inference through a linear-programming relaxation and parameter learning through a structured support vector machine. These components address both how to compute a segmentation and how to learn the parameters governing it. Experiments on multiple datasets show the higher-order method outperforming other state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms. The reported contribution combines richer relationships between image regions with an inference and learning framework that makes those relationships usable.
neurips-2011-higher-order-correlation-cl.tldr: Higher-order correlation clustering uses group relationships among superpixels to improve segmentation around ambiguous boundaries.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much information populations of spiking neurons carry and how that information can be decoded optimally. It applies asymptotic statistical-inference theory to large populations carrying a finite total amount of information. Under this setup, the authors establish a simpler description of the information contained in the full population response.

Asymptotically, that response is as informative as one observation from a Gaussian process. Its mean and covariance are explicitly related to network and individual-neuron properties. In certain cases, this Gaussian representation enables optimal Bayesian decoding through simple linear transformations and yields closed-form expressions for the network's Shannon information.

The theory also accommodates non-Poisson network models, including neurons whose activity depends strongly on their histories. Under some conditions, such populations carry exactly the same information as equivalent populations of independent Poisson neurons with matched firing rates. The qualifications matter: this equivalence is conditional, and the Gaussian result is asymptotic. Within those settings, the findings help explain neural decoding results and questions relevant to neuroprosthetic design.
neurips-2011-information-rates-and-optim.tldr: For large neural populations with finite total information, an asymptotically equivalent Gaussian representation can simplify information calculations and optimal decoding.

paragraphs: Writers often omit facts they expect readers to infer using shared knowledge. This creates a particular missing-data problem for learning rules from text: omitted facts are related to what the reader is presumed to know. The paper uses that relationship as information about the underlying domain knowledge.

The authors introduce a mention model that assigns probabilities to facts appearing in a text, given previously mentioned facts and domain knowledge expressed as Horn clause rules. Learning jointly searches for rules and estimates the mention model's parameters. An Expectation Maximization procedure within a Markov Logic framework performs this combined inference.

Experiments on synthetic and natural text show that the method learns accurate rules and applies them to new texts to make correct inferences. It also outperforms a standard EM approach that treats mentions as missing at random. The result supports explicitly modeling why information is left unstated: when omission reflects expected inference, accounting for that process can help recover the knowledge that made concise communication possible.
neurips-2011-inverting-grice-s-maxims-to.tldr: A probabilistic model of why writers omit inferable facts helps learn domain rules from concise text.

paragraphs: Agglomerative clustering builds groups through a sequence of merges, choosing the most similar pair at each step. Its behavior therefore depends heavily on the similarity function. This paper develops a way to learn that function from ground-truth clustered data rather than designing the merge criterion entirely by hand.

The authors treat similarity as the action-value function of a reinforcement learning problem. This frames the evaluation of a possible merge within the clustering process itself. They apply the general method to image segmentation by merging superpixels, calling the resulting approach Learning to Agglomerate Superpixel Hierarchies, or LASH.

On a challenging dataset of brain images from serial electron microscopy, LASH dramatically improves segmentation accuracy when clustering supervoxels produced by state-of-the-art boundary detectors. Directly training supervoxel similarities and then applying single-linkage clustering produces a smaller improvement. The comparison supports learning the criterion as part of the sequential merging problem: the contribution concerns how existing image regions are assembled into larger segments, building on the initial boundary detection.
neurips-2011-learning-to-agglomerate-sup.tldr: LASH learns a clustering similarity function as a reinforcement-learning action value and substantially improves segmentation of electron-microscopy brain images.

paragraphs: Markov random fields can estimate data distributions and supply features for classification, but their partition function can be difficult to estimate. This quantity normalizes the model's probabilities. The paper develops a method that follows the log partition function as a restricted Boltzmann machine is trained, taking advantage of the successive gradient updates.

The method combines two information sources: estimates of the change caused by each update and bridge-sampling estimates of differences across a small collection of tempered distributions. An inference procedure resembling Kalman filtering integrates these estimates. When training uses Tempered Stochastic Maximum Likelihood, the approach needs no additional temperatures beyond those already required for learning.

Across several datasets, comparisons with exact values and annealed importance sampling show accurate tracking of the log partition function. Unlike the latter comparison method, the proposed approach supplies an estimate at every training step with computational cost similar to training alone. Its practical contribution is to make normalization estimates available throughout learning while reusing information generated by the training process.
neurips-2011-on-tracking-the-partition-f.tldr: Combining update-based estimates with bridge sampling tracks an RBM's log partition function throughout learning at a cost similar to training alone.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an online prediction problem in which an algorithm repeatedly chooses an ordering of items. After each choice, a monotone submodular function is revealed. The ordering incurs a loss equal to how far along the sequence the algorithm must go before satisfying the function's coverage requirement.

This formulation makes early coverage the objective: two sequences containing the same items can have different losses because useful items appear in different positions. The authors develop a learning algorithm whose loss converges approximately to that of the best single sequence chosen in hindsight. The comparison therefore asks how well repeated prediction can approach an ordering selected with knowledge of the observed tasks.

The framework connects submodular set cover with ranking and repeated active learning. The proposed algorithm also extends to rounds revealing multiple functions and to bandit and contextual bandit settings. These extensions broaden the kinds of feedback and task information the approach can accommodate. The stated guarantee is an approximate comparison with the hindsight sequence, rather than exact equality with that benchmark.
neurips-2011-online-submodular-set-cover.tldr: An online algorithm learns item orderings whose coverage loss approaches that of the best hindsight ordering up to approximation.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to combine multiple image cues within a bag-of-words representation for classification. It builds compound visual words from primitive cues learned independently from training images. These compound words let the representation capture useful combinations of cues while keeping the resulting vocabulary compact.

The approach rests on the observation that constructing joint-cue models from independently modeled cues is more statistically robust for typical classification problems than directly estimating the full dependent joint distribution. Information-theoretic vocabulary compression identifies discriminative cue combinations. The resulting portmanteau words bind cues together while still allowing individual cues to receive separate weights in the final representation.

Experiments achieve state-of-the-art results on the Oxford Flower-102 and Caltech-UCSD Bird-200 datasets. The authors use these findings to demonstrate effectiveness relative to substantially more complex approaches for representing multiple cues. The central contribution is a compact way to preserve useful cue combinations without directly estimating every dependency from the training data. The robustness observation is framed around typical classification settings, and the performance evidence comes from the two stated datasets.
neurips-2011-portmanteau-vocabularies-fo.tldr: Compact compound visual vocabularies combine independently learned cues and achieve state-of-the-art results on flower and bird classification datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction of node labels on graphs, focusing on weighted trees. Trees are useful because spanning-tree sparsification can preserve information from a larger graph while simplifying prediction. Although nearly optimal methods were already known for unweighted trees, the authors identify a gap in the corresponding weighted setting.

They introduce Shazoo, an efficient predictor that is nearly optimal on any weighted tree. The algorithm also provides a common, nontrivial generalization of earlier approaches for unweighted trees and weighted lines. This unification matters because it brings together branching structure and edge weights within one prediction method.

Experiments on real-world datasets show that Shazoo makes effective use of the input tree's structure. Its performance comes close to that of less scalable energy-minimization methods and sometimes exceeds them. The contribution combines a theoretical guarantee for weighted trees with evidence of practical predictive strength. The empirical comparisons do not establish that it always beats energy minimization, but they support its usefulness as an efficient tree-based approach.
neurips-2011-see-the-tree-through-the-li.tldr: Shazoo efficiently predicts node labels on weighted trees with near-optimal guarantees and competitive real-world performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when the agent is given several possible ways to summarize its observation history into a finite state. At least one candidate is assumed to produce genuinely Markovian dynamics, meaning that its current state supplies the relevant history for the resulting decision process. The agent does not know which candidate has this property.

The agent also lacks the probabilistic characteristics of the Markov decision process induced by a correct representation. It must therefore learn how to act while resolving uncertainty about how its observations should be represented. The performance target is the optimal policy for a correct model, or the best correct model when several candidates qualify.

The authors propose an algorithm with regret of order T^(2/3), where T is the time horizon. Because this grows more slowly than T, the average reward shortfall relative to the target decreases with the horizon at the stated order. The result supplies a learning guarantee despite representation uncertainty, conditional on the candidate collection containing at least one Markovian representation.
neurips-2011-selecting-the-state-represe.tldr: An algorithm learns among candidate state representations with order T^(2/3) regret, assuming at least one candidate yields Markovian dynamics.

paragraphs: The paper uses RGB-D images, which combine color and depth, to construct three-dimensional point clouds of indoor scenes and assign semantic labels to their segments. Its graphical model incorporates local appearance and shape alongside contextual information: which objects occur together and how objects are positioned geometrically.

To keep a model with many object classes and relationships parsimonious, the authors use multiple types of edge potentials. These encode different relationships within the graphical model. The formulation supports efficient approximate inference, and its parameters are trained through maximum-margin learning. This combines evidence about individual regions with evidence about their surroundings.

The experiments cover 52 home and office scenes assembled from roughly 550 views, with 2,495 segments labeled across 27 classes. The authors report labeling performance of 84.06% for 17 office classes and 73.38% for 17 home classes. They also successfully apply the algorithms to a mobile robot searching for objects in large, cluttered rooms. The results demonstrate the approach in both scene labeling and a practical robotic task.
neurips-2011-semantic-labeling-of-3d-poi.tldr: A graphical model combines appearance, shape, and object relationships to label indoor 3D scenes and support robotic object finding.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the representational value of depth in sum-product networks. These are computation networks whose units calculate either products or weighted sums. The authors compare architectures with multiple hidden layers against shallow architectures with one hidden layer, asking how many hidden units are needed to represent the same functions.

Their theoretical result identifies families of functions that deep sum-product networks can represent with substantially fewer hidden units than shallow ones. This establishes an efficiency advantage for depth within those families. The relevant resource is representation size: adding layers can reduce the number of units required to express particular computations.

The finding supplies a mathematical motivation for studying and learning deep sum-product networks, and the authors connect it more broadly to interest in deep learning. Its claim is existential: there are function families for which depth provides a strong advantage. The contribution is therefore a separation in representational power, rather than an empirical claim that every deep model will learn better than every shallow model.
neurips-2011-shallow-vs-deep-sum-product.tldr: Some function families require substantially fewer hidden units in deep sum-product networks than in single-hidden-layer networks.

paragraphs: Tracking cells in time-lapse microscopy requires following many similar-looking objects across an image sequence. Reliable tracks matter for studying cell cultures and development. The paper observes that existing methods often use only a small feature set so that their parameters remain manageable through manual adjustment or grid search.

The authors propose learning the tracking parameters automatically from a training set using structured learning. This changes the practical constraint on the representation: a richer set of features can be included because their parameters no longer all need to be tuned by hand. Parameter learning is thus central to expanding the information available to the tracker.

On two public benchmark sequences, the approach improves tracking compared with recently reported methods. The stated findings link automatic parameter estimation to the successful use of richer features in a task involving many homogeneous objects. The paper's contribution is a learned tracking framework supported by those benchmark comparisons, showing how training data can help manage a more expressive model for microscopy sequences.
neurips-2011-structured-learning-for-cel.tldr: Structured learning automatically tunes a richer cell-tracking model and improves results on two public microscopy benchmarks.

paragraphs: Approximate inference makes it possible to work with probabilistic graphical models whose exact calculations are intractable. This paper extends that idea from models based on the exponential family to the t-exponential family. The extension requires a suitable way to measure differences between distributions within the new mathematical setting.

The authors define a t-divergence for this purpose. They derive it through convex duality connecting the t-exponential family's log-partition function with a newly introduced t-entropy. This construction ties the divergence to the structure of the distribution family, giving the proposed inference approach a common mathematical foundation with its normalization and entropy quantities.

The paper illustrates the approach using a Bayes Point Machine with a Student's t-prior. That example shows how the proposed construction can enter a probabilistic learning model using this prior. The stated contribution is the extension and its mathematical formulation, accompanied by an illustration. It provides a way to formulate approximate inference in the t-exponential setting, with the example serving to demonstrate its use.
neurips-2011-t-divergence-based-approxim.tldr: A new t-divergence derived through convex duality extends approximate inference to the t-exponential family.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how quickly boosting approaches the lowest possible empirical risk for a broad class of losses, including exponential and logistic losses. A central difficulty is that the risk's infimum may not be attained by any available solution. The analysis explicitly addresses this obstacle rather than assuming a minimizer exists.

Under weak learnability, the authors establish a convergence rate of order ln(1/ε) for the whole loss class. They also characterize a separate set of conditions, based on the sample and weak learning class, under which the infimum is attainable. For that setting, they provide a new proof of the known logarithmic rate.

The authors then show that any instance can be decomposed into two smaller instances resembling those special cases. This yields a general rate of order 1/ε, improving the previously available order exp(1/ε²) rate. A matching lower bound for logistic loss shows that the general rate cannot be improved in order for that loss. The work therefore explains both favorable special cases and a sharper general convergence guarantee.
neurips-2011-the-fast-convergence-of-boo.tldr: A decomposition of boosting problems yields a general O(1/ε) convergence rate, with faster special cases and a matching logistic-loss lower bound.
